extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, media-policy researchers, and anyone interested in journalism ethics and media independence
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether a news outlet or publication is free to make content decisions (what, how, when to report) without external influence, and identifying legal, institutional, and practical protections or indicators of compromised independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to make content decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial independence refers to the freedom of journalists and media organizations to make content decisions—such as what to report, how to report it, and when to report it—without external influence from owners, governments, advertisers, or other outside forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core definitional standard: evaluate whether editors/journalists can decide coverage, framing, and timing absent intervention by owners, state actors, advertisers, or other external pressures. Examples of outside forces to watch for include owners, governments, and advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and policy protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries that want to foster an independent media ecosystem and protect editorial independence often pursue laws against concentration of media ownership and provide subsidies for independent media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing independence, consider whether legal frameworks and public policies exist that (a) limit media ownership concentration and (b) provide financial support mechanisms that reduce dependence on hostile owners or advertisers. Presence/absence of these measures is a structural criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling should reflect editorial independence (not merely funding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and public broadcasters with editorial independence object to labeling that focuses on whether or not they get funding from a government as misleading audiences to believe that it impacts their coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good practice for platforms and regulators is to base 'state media' or similar labels on actual editorial control and independence rather than only on funding sources. The article cites Twitter's prior refusal to label the BBC as 'state-affiliated' because of its editorial independence, and the backlash when labeling practices changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish funding sources from editorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial independence is what readers really want to know; funding source alone can be a misleading proxy for independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should ask: does government (or another funder) exert editorial control, or is funding provided without interference? Examples in the article: platform labeling controversies (Twitter/YouTube) where funding-focused labels drew criticism for conflating funding with control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of compromised editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Events and actions that signal erosion of independence include owners intervening in editorial decisions, spiking of endorsements or coverage, state control of media, and public protests against propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concrete incidents (e.g., management spiking an endorsement, state takeover or control, organized protests, or policy changes that enable interference) as evidence the outlet's editorial independence is compromised. The article cites the Washington Post endorsement spiking, protests in Hungary, and controversies over labeling as illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of independence in student and small publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Student publications also have a range of editorial independence from their schools, some of which try to prevent any negative publicity that the student journalists might uncover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree of institutional control in student and campus media separately: some have full editorial autonomy, others face administrative pressure or censorship. Consider governance rules, funding sources, and school policies when assessing independence in these contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence as a normative journalistic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a sacrosanct principle for independent media organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging newsroom practices or policies, weigh editorial independence as a fundamental ethical norm. Threats to independence should be treated as serious harms to journalistic integrity and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence as an institutional design concept across functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Other public functions are often granted institutional independence (e.g., central bank independence, civil service independence, judicial independence), indicating independence is a broader governance design principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this comparative perspective to evaluate whether mechanisms that secure independence in other institutions (formal legal protections, insulated governance structures, tenure/stability provisions) are present or could be adapted to media organizations to strengthen editorial independence.
